cards.q: Contrast a physical change with a chemical change at the particulate level.
cards.a: Physical change: only the attractions between particles are disrupted; the particles themselves are unchanged (melting, boiling, dissolving). Chemical change: bonds within particles break and new bonds form, so different substances exist afterward.
cards.note: Dissolving NaCl in water is classified as a physical change on the AP exam even though the ions separate.

cards.q: Identify the macroscopic evidence that a chemical change has occurred.
cards.a: Gas evolved that is not simply boiling, a precipitate forming, a permanent color change, a temperature change with no external heating, light emitted, or a new odor. Confirmation requires showing a new substance is present.
cards.note: Bubbles alone can mean boiling; AP wants evidence tied to the formation of a new substance.

cards.q: Explain why dissolving an ionic solid in water is treated as a physical change.
cards.a: Water molecules pull the ions apart by ion-dipole attraction. The ions are chemically unchanged and can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the water, so only interparticle attractions were disrupted.

cards.q: Define a net ionic equation.
cards.a: An equation showing only the species that actually change: soluble strong electrolytes are written as separated aqueous ions and all spectator ions are cancelled. Both mass and total charge must balance.
cards.hint: → what is kept, what is cancelled
cards.note: Charge balance is scored separately; a net ionic equation with unbalanced charge earns no credit.

cards.q: Define a spectator ion.
cards.a: An ion that is present in the same aqueous, unchanged form both before and after the reaction, so it cancels out of the complete ionic equation and does not appear in the net ionic equation.

cards.q: State which species are written as separated ions and which are kept as complete formulas in an ionic equation.
cards.a: Separate: strong acids, strong bases, and soluble ionic salts labeled (aq). Keep intact: all solids (s), liquids (l), gases (g), weak acids, weak bases, and molecular compounds such as water.
cards.note: Writing a weak acid such as CH3COOH as separated ions is one of the most common AP scoring errors.

cards.q: Write the net ionic equation for aqueous silver nitrate mixed with aqueous sodium chloride.
cards.a: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). Sodium ion and nitrate ion are spectators and are omitted.

cards.q: State the solubility guidelines most often required on the AP Chemistry exam.
cards.a: Always soluble: Group 1 cations, NH4⁺, NO3⁻, ClO4⁻, and most acetates. Generally insoluble: most carbonates, phosphates, sulfides, and hydroxides, plus the halides of Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, and Hg2²⁺.
cards.note: No solubility table is provided on the exam, so the always-soluble rules must be memorized.

cards.q: Explain what makes a solute a strong electrolyte and why that matters for ionic equations.
cards.a: A strong electrolyte dissociates essentially completely into free ions in water (strong acids, strong bases, soluble salts). Because it truly exists as separate ions in solution, it is written in separated ionic form.

cards.q: Explain what a particulate diagram drawn after a precipitation reaction must show.
cards.a: The precipitate drawn as a neutral cluster of alternating cations and anions, the spectator ions still drawn as separate hydrated ions in correct relative numbers, and any leftover excess reactant ions still in solution.
cards.note: Students routinely forget to draw the excess reactant ions that survive after the limiting reactant is used up.

cards.q: State the relationship used to convert between mass and moles of a substance.
cards.a: n = m / M, where n is moles, m is mass in grams, and M is molar mass in g/mol. Mole ratios taken from the balanced equation then connect moles of one species to moles of another.

cards.q: Explain why the coefficients of a balanced equation give mole ratios rather than mass ratios.
cards.a: Coefficients count particles, and a mole is a fixed number of particles. Masses of equal particle counts differ because molar masses differ, so masses must be converted to moles before the ratio is applied.

cards.q: Define the limiting reactant and state how to identify it.
cards.a: The reactant consumed completely first, which sets the maximum amount of product. Identify it by dividing the moles of each reactant by its coefficient in the balanced equation; the smallest quotient is the limiting reactant.
cards.note: Compare moles divided by coefficients, never raw masses and never raw moles.

cards.q: State how to find the amount of excess reactant remaining after a reaction goes to completion.
cards.a: Remaining moles = initial moles of the excess reactant minus the moles consumed, where moles consumed = moles of limiting reactant times the coefficient ratio. Multiply by molar mass if grams are requested.

cards.q: Define theoretical yield, actual yield, and percent yield.
cards.a: Theoretical yield is the maximum product predicted from the limiting reactant. Actual yield is the mass really recovered. Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%.

cards.q: Explain why an experimental percent yield is usually below 100%.
cards.a: The reaction may be incomplete or reversible, competing side reactions may consume reactant, product is lost during transfer and filtration, and some product may stay dissolved in the solvent.
cards.note: A percent yield above 100% indicates impure or incompletely dried product, not a better reaction.

cards.q: State the definition of molarity and its equation.
cards.a: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution: M = mol solute / L solution, with units mol/L.
cards.note: The volume is liters of final solution, not liters of solvent added.

cards.q: State the dilution relationship and the reason it works.
cards.a: M1V1 = M2V2. Adding solvent does not change the moles of solute, so concentration falls in exact proportion to the increase in solution volume.

cards.q: Determine the concentration of sulfate ion in 0.10 M Al2(SO4)3.
cards.a: 0.30 M. Each formula unit releases three SO4²⁻ ions, so [SO4²⁻] = 3 x 0.10 M. The aluminum ion concentration is 0.20 M.
cards.note: Forgetting to multiply by the ion subscript is a classic concentration trap.

cards.q: State the full sequence of steps for a mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem with a limiting reactant.
cards.a: Balance the equation; convert each reactant mass to moles; divide each by its coefficient and take the smallest to find the limiting reactant; use the mole ratio to get moles of product; multiply by the molar mass of the product.

cards.q: Define a titration.
cards.a: A procedure in which a solution of accurately known concentration (the titrant) is delivered from a burette into a measured volume of analyte until the reaction is exactly complete, allowing the unknown concentration to be calculated.

cards.q: Contrast the equivalence point with the endpoint of a titration.
cards.a: The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point at which moles of titrant exactly satisfy the balanced equation. The endpoint is the observed indicator color change used to approximate it; the gap between them is titration error.
cards.note: These are not synonyms; free response questions often ask which one the indicator actually signals.

cards.q: State the general procedure for finding an unknown concentration from titration data.
cards.a: Compute moles of titrant as M x V; convert to moles of analyte using the mole ratio from the balanced equation; divide by the analyte volume in liters to get its molarity.
cards.note: MaVa = MbVb is valid only for a 1:1 mole ratio; otherwise the coefficients must be included.

cards.q: Explain the effect on the calculated result of rinsing a burette with distilled water instead of with titrant.
cards.a: The titrant in the burette is diluted, so a larger volume is delivered before the endpoint. The calculated moles of titrant, and therefore the reported analyte concentration, come out too high.
cards.note: Rinsing the receiving flask with water is harmless because the moles of analyte in it are unchanged.

cards.q: Define a primary standard and explain what standardizing a solution means.
cards.a: A primary standard is a pure, stable, accurately weighable solid used to prepare a solution of exactly known concentration. Standardizing means titrating another solution against it to determine that solution's true concentration.

cards.q: Decide how to choose an appropriate indicator for an acid-base titration.
cards.a: Choose an indicator whose color-change range brackets the pH at the equivalence point: phenolphthalein for a weak acid titrated with strong base or for strong-strong, methyl orange for a weak base titrated with strong acid.

cards.q: Define gravimetric analysis.
cards.a: A quantitative technique in which an excess of a precipitating reagent removes the target ion as an insoluble solid; the precipitate is filtered, dried, and weighed, and its mass is converted to moles of the target ion in the original sample.
cards.note: The precipitating reagent must be in excess so that essentially all of the target ion is captured.

cards.q: Explain why a gravimetric precipitate must be washed and dried to constant mass.
cards.a: Washing removes soluble spectator ions clinging to the crystals and drying removes residual water. Both would otherwise add mass, making the calculated amount of analyte too large.

cards.q: Identify the three broad categories of chemical reaction emphasized in AP Chemistry.
cards.a: Acid-base reactions (proton transfer), precipitation reactions (formation of an insoluble ionic solid), and oxidation-reduction reactions (electron transfer).
cards.hint: → three names with the transferred species

cards.q: Define a precipitation reaction and illustrate its net ionic form.
cards.a: Two soluble ionic solutions are mixed and oppositely charged ions combine into an insoluble solid. Example: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s).

cards.q: Predict whether mixing aqueous sodium sulfate with aqueous barium nitrate gives a precipitate, and write the net ionic equation.
cards.a: Yes, barium sulfate precipitates: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s). Sodium ion and nitrate ion are spectators.

cards.q: Define a Bronsted-Lowry acid and a Bronsted-Lowry base.
cards.a: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Every such reaction transfers H⁺ from the acid to the base, producing a conjugate base and a conjugate acid.

cards.q: State the net ionic equation for the neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base.
cards.a: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l), equivalently H3O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2 H2O(l).
cards.note: If either the acid or the base is weak, the weak species stays intact in the net ionic equation.

cards.q: Predict the products formed when a strong acid is added to a metal carbonate.
cards.a: Carbon dioxide gas, water, and the dissolved salt. For an insoluble carbonate: CaCO3(s) + 2 H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g).
cards.note: Carbonic acid is unstable and decomposes, so H2CO3 should not be left as a final product.

cards.q: Define a combustion reaction and state the products of complete hydrocarbon combustion.
cards.a: A rapid exothermic reaction with O2. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon yields CO2 and H2O; incomplete combustion with limited oxygen yields CO or soot as well.

cards.q: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons and oxidation numbers.
cards.a: Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation number; reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation number. The two always occur together (LEO says GER).

cards.q: State the rules for assigning oxidation numbers.
cards.a: Free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge; the sum is 0 for a neutral compound and equals the charge for a polyatomic ion; Group 1 = +1, Group 2 = +2, F = -1; H = +1 except -1 with metals; O = -2 except -1 in peroxides and +2 in OF2.
cards.note: The rules apply in priority order, so fluorine and Groups 1 and 2 outrank the hydrogen and oxygen rules.

cards.q: Determine the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, Cr2O7²⁻.
cards.a: +6. The seven oxygens contribute 7(-2) = -14, and the total must equal -2, so 2x - 14 = -2 and x = +6.

cards.q: Identify how to tell the oxidizing agent from the reducing agent in a redox reaction.
cards.a: The oxidizing agent is the species that is reduced: it gains electrons and its oxidation number decreases. The reducing agent is the species that is oxidized: it loses electrons and its oxidation number increases.
cards.note: The labels run opposite to intuition; each agent undergoes the process named after the other.

cards.q: Decide quickly whether a given reaction is an oxidation-reduction reaction.
cards.a: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom on both sides; if any element changes oxidation number, the reaction is redox. Reactions involving a free element on one side are almost always redox.
cards.note: Double-replacement precipitations and acid-base neutralizations are never redox reactions.

cards.q: Define disproportionation.
cards.a: A redox reaction in which one element in a single oxidation state is simultaneously oxidized and reduced, ending up in both a higher and a lower oxidation state.

cards.q: State the half-reaction method for balancing a redox equation in acidic solution.
cards.a: Split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions; balance all elements except O and H; add H2O to balance oxygen; add H⁺ to balance hydrogen; add electrons to balance charge; scale the halves so electrons cancel; add them together.
cards.note: Balance oxygen with water first and only then hydrogen with H⁺; the reverse order does not work.

cards.q: State the extra step needed to balance a redox equation in basic solution.
cards.a: Balance the equation first as if it were acidic, then add to both sides as many OH⁻ as there are H⁺. Combine H⁺ + OH⁻ into H2O on that side and cancel any water appearing on both sides.

cards.q: Balance in acidic solution: MnO4⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺.
cards.a: MnO4⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H2O + 5 Fe³⁺. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons, so five Fe²⁺ are oxidized.

cards.q: Explain the two quantities that must be conserved in a balanced redox equation.
cards.a: Mass, meaning the atoms of every element match on both sides, and charge, meaning the total charge on the left equals the total charge on the right. Equivalently, electrons lost must equal electrons gained.

cards.q: Define the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.a: The change in the concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, usually in mol/(L·s). It is reported as a positive number, so reactant concentration changes carry a negative sign in the definition.

cards.q: State how the rates of the individual species relate for the reaction aA + bB → cC + dD.
cards.a: rate = -(1/a)Δ[A]/Δt = -(1/b)Δ[B]/Δt = (1/c)Δ[C]/Δt = (1/d)Δ[D]/Δt. Dividing by each coefficient produces a single rate value for the whole reaction.
cards.note: Species with larger coefficients change concentration faster, not slower.

cards.q: For 2 N2O5 → 4 NO2 + O2, oxygen appears at 0.020 M/s. Determine the rate at which N2O5 disappears.
cards.a: 0.040 M/s. The stoichiometric ratio of N2O5 to O2 is 2 to 1, so -Δ[N2O5]/Δt = 2 x 0.020 M/s.

cards.q: Explain why the rate of most reactions decreases as the reaction proceeds.
cards.a: Reactant concentrations fall as they are consumed, so productive collisions become less frequent. Because rate depends on concentration through the rate law, the instantaneous rate declines toward zero.

cards.q: Identify the factors that change the rate of a chemical reaction.
cards.a: Concentration or partial pressure of reactants, temperature, surface area of any solid reactant, the physical state and degree of mixing, and the presence of a catalyst.
cards.note: A catalyst changes the rate but never changes ΔH, ΔG, or the position of equilibrium.

cards.q: Explain why increasing the surface area of a solid reactant speeds up a reaction.
cards.a: Reaction can occur only where particles meet the exposed surface. Grinding the solid into powder exposes far more particles at once, raising the number of collisions per second without changing any concentration.

cards.q: Explain why a modest increase in temperature produces a large increase in reaction rate.
cards.a: Higher temperature shifts the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution toward higher energies, so a much larger fraction of collisions carry at least the activation energy. Collision frequency rises slightly too, but the exponential energy factor dominates.

cards.q: Define a rate law.
cards.a: An experimentally determined equation expressing rate in terms of reactant concentrations, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are the reaction orders and k is the temperature-dependent rate constant.

cards.q: Define reaction order and overall reaction order.
cards.a: The order with respect to a species is the exponent on that species concentration in the rate law. The overall order is the sum of all the exponents. Orders are usually 0, 1, or 2 but may be fractional.

cards.q: Explain why the exponents in a rate law cannot be read from the balanced overall equation.
cards.a: The rate law reflects only the rate-determining elementary step, not the overall stoichiometry. Orders must be measured experimentally or derived from a proposed mechanism; only a single elementary step may use its own coefficients.
cards.note: Copying the balanced coefficients into the rate law is among the most heavily penalized AP errors.

cards.q: State the units of the rate constant k for zero-, first-, and second-order reactions.
cards.a: Zero order: M/s. First order: s⁻¹. Second order: M⁻¹s⁻¹. In general the units are M^(1-n)·s⁻¹ for an overall order n.
cards.note: The units of k by themselves can reveal the overall order on a multiple-choice question.

cards.q: State how to determine reaction orders from a table of initial-rate data.
cards.a: Compare two trials in which only one reactant concentration changes. If that concentration is multiplied by f and the rate is multiplied by f raised to m, the order in that reactant is m. Repeat for each reactant, then substitute one trial to find k.
cards.note: Only vary one concentration at a time; choosing trials where two concentrations change gives a wrong order.

cards.q: Determine the order in A when doubling [A] at constant [B] multiplies the rate by four.
cards.a: Second order in A, because 2 raised to m equals 4 requires m = 2.

cards.q: State the integrated rate law for a zero-order reaction and the plot that is linear.
cards.a: $[A]_{t} - [A]_{0} = -kt$. A plot of [A] versus time is a straight line with slope -k and intercept [A]0.

cards.q: State the integrated rate law for a first-order reaction and the plot that is linear.
cards.a: $\ln [A]_{t} - \ln [A]_{0} = -kt$. A plot of ln[A] versus time is a straight line with slope -k.

cards.q: State the integrated rate law for a second-order reaction and the plot that is linear.
cards.a: $\frac{1}{[A]_{t}} - \frac{1}{[A]_{0}} = kt$. A plot of 1/[A] versus time is a straight line with slope +k.
cards.note: The second-order slope is positive, while the zero- and first-order slopes are negative.

cards.q: Identify the reaction order from which concentration-versus-time plot comes out linear.
cards.a: A straight line for [A] vs t means zero order; for ln[A] vs t means first order; for 1/[A] vs t means second order. The order is whichever transformation linearizes the data.
cards.note: AP frequently supplies all three plots and asks which one is straight.

cards.q: Define half-life and give the half-life expression for a first-order reaction.
cards.a: The half-life is the time for the reactant concentration to fall to half its current value. For a first-order reaction $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$, which is independent of the starting concentration.

cards.q: Explain why a constant half-life identifies a reaction as first order.
cards.a: Only for first order does the half-life expression contain no concentration term. Zero-order half-lives grow shorter as the reaction proceeds and second-order half-lives grow longer, so equal successive half-lives means first order.

cards.q: Determine the fraction of a first-order reactant remaining after n half-lives.
cards.a: (1/2) raised to the n. After three half-lives 12.5% remains; after four, 6.25%.

cards.q: Define the collision model of reaction rates.
cards.a: Reactant particles must physically collide to react. The rate equals the collision frequency multiplied by the fraction of collisions that are effective, and only collisions with sufficient energy and correct orientation produce product.

cards.q: State the two requirements for a collision to result in reaction.
cards.a: The colliding particles must have combined kinetic energy at least equal to the activation energy, and they must be oriented so that the atoms that need to bond actually meet.

cards.q: Define activation energy.
cards.a: The minimum energy colliding particles must possess to reach the transition state and go on to products. On an energy profile it is the vertical rise from the reactants to the peak.

cards.q: Define the activated complex and distinguish it from an intermediate.
cards.a: The activated complex, or transition state, is the highest-energy arrangement at the peak of the profile with old bonds partly broken and new bonds partly formed. It cannot be isolated, whereas an intermediate sits in an energy minimum and can be.

cards.q: State the Arrhenius equation and identify each symbol.
cards.a: $k = A e^{-E_{a}/(RT)}$, where A is the frequency factor including collision orientation, Ea is the activation energy, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), and T is the absolute temperature.
cards.note: Ea must be expressed in joules per mole when R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is used.

cards.q: State the linear form of the Arrhenius equation and how activation energy is extracted from it.
cards.a: $\ln k = -\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right) + \ln A$. A plot of ln k versus 1/T is a straight line of slope -Ea/R with intercept ln A, so Ea = -R times the slope.

cards.q: A plot of ln k versus 1/T has slope -1.2 x 10⁴ K. Determine the activation energy.
cards.a: Ea = -R x slope = -(8.314)(-1.2 x 10⁴) = 1.0 x 10⁵ J/mol, about 1.0 x 10² kJ/mol.
cards.note: A negative slope must yield a positive Ea; a negative activation energy signals a dropped sign.

cards.q: Explain how a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows the effect of temperature on rate.
cards.a: The curve plots the number of particles against kinetic energy. Raising the temperature lowers and broadens the peak and shifts it right, greatly increasing the area beyond Ea, which is the fraction of particles able to react.

cards.q: Explain how adding a catalyst is represented on a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
cards.a: The distribution curve itself is unchanged; the vertical Ea line moves to the left to a lower value, so a larger area under the curve, meaning a larger fraction of particles, now exceeds it.
cards.hint: → what moves and what does not
cards.note: A catalyst does not give particles more energy; it lowers the energy bar they must clear.

cards.q: Define a reaction mechanism.
cards.a: The sequence of elementary steps by which reactants are converted to products. The steps must sum to the overall balanced equation and must predict the experimentally observed rate law.

cards.q: Define an elementary step and state how its rate law is written.
cards.a: An elementary step is a single molecular event that occurs exactly as written. Its rate law follows directly from its own coefficients, so A + B → products gives rate = k[A][B] and 2A → products gives rate = k[A]².
cards.note: Only for elementary steps may exponents be taken from coefficients.

cards.q: Define molecularity and name its three types.
cards.a: Molecularity is the number of particles that collide in an elementary step. Unimolecular involves one particle, bimolecular two, and termolecular three; termolecular steps are rare because simultaneous three-body collisions are very unlikely.

cards.q: Define a reaction intermediate.
cards.a: A species produced in one elementary step and consumed in a later step, so it cancels and does not appear in the overall balanced equation. Unlike a transition state it occupies an energy minimum and can sometimes be detected.
cards.note: An intermediate may never appear in a final rate law; it must be substituted away.

cards.q: Define the rate-determining step.
cards.a: The slowest elementary step in a mechanism. It acts as a bottleneck, so the observed rate law matches the rate law of that step once any intermediate has been eliminated.

cards.q: State the predicted rate law when the first elementary step of a mechanism is the slow step.
cards.a: The overall rate law is simply the rate law of that first step, written from its molecularity, because every later step is fast. For a slow A + B → C, the rate law is rate = k[A][B].

cards.q: Explain how to derive the rate law when a fast reversible step precedes the rate-determining step.
cards.a: Write the rate law of the slow step, then eliminate the intermediate: set the forward and reverse rates of the fast equilibrium equal, solve for the intermediate concentration in terms of reactants, and substitute. The constants merge into one observed k.
cards.hint: → set forward equal to reverse, then substitute
cards.note: The final rate law must contain only reactants, or a catalyst, and never an intermediate.

cards.q: Explain why an intermediate cannot appear in an experimentally determined rate law.
cards.a: Rate laws are found by varying measurable initial concentrations, but an intermediate is absent at the start and cannot be controlled by the experimenter, so its concentration must be re-expressed in terms of reactants.

cards.q: State the two criteria a proposed mechanism must satisfy to be acceptable.
cards.a: The elementary steps must add up to the overall balanced equation with all intermediates cancelling, and the mechanism must predict the rate law that is observed experimentally.

cards.q: Define a catalyst.
cards.a: A substance that increases reaction rate by providing an alternative mechanism with a lower activation energy. It is consumed in an early step and regenerated in a later step, so it is not used up overall and does not appear in the balanced equation.

cards.q: State what a catalyst does change and what it does not change.
cards.a: Changes: the mechanism, the activation energy (lowered for forward and reverse alike), the rate constant, and the rate. Does not change: ΔH, ΔE, ΔG, the equilibrium constant, the equilibrium position, or the final amount of product.
cards.note: A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but is not shifted.

cards.q: Contrast a homogeneous catalyst with a heterogeneous catalyst.
cards.a: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants, such as aqueous acid catalyzing a reaction in solution. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, typically a solid surface on which gaseous reactants adsorb, react, and desorb.

cards.q: Explain how an enzyme catalyzes a biological reaction.
cards.a: The substrate binds in the enzyme's active site, which holds it in a favorable orientation and stabilizes the transition state, lowering the activation energy. The enzyme is released unchanged and is highly specific to its substrate.

cards.q: Identify the forward activation energy, reverse activation energy, and ΔH on a reaction energy profile.
cards.a: Ea forward is the peak height measured up from the reactants; Ea reverse is the peak height measured up from the products; ΔH is the product energy minus the reactant energy. Therefore ΔH = Ea(forward) - Ea(reverse).
cards.note: Products lying below reactants means the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.

cards.q: Identify the rate-determining step from a multi-step reaction energy profile.
cards.a: Each hump is one elementary step. The rate-determining step is the one with the largest activation energy, measured as the climb from the valley immediately before it up to its own peak.
cards.note: Use the height of the climb from the preceding valley, not the absolute height of the peak above the axis.

cards.q: Explain what the valleys between peaks on a multi-step energy profile represent.
cards.a: They are reaction intermediates: real species at a local energy minimum that are formed in one elementary step and consumed in the next.

cards.q: Contrast endothermic and exothermic processes.
cards.a: Endothermic: the system absorbs energy, q > 0 and ΔH > 0, products lie above reactants in energy, and the surroundings cool. Exothermic: the system releases energy, q < 0 and ΔH < 0, products lie below reactants, and the surroundings warm.
cards.hint: → signs plus temperature of the surroundings

cards.q: Define system and surroundings in a thermochemistry problem.
cards.a: The system is the portion of the universe being studied, normally the reacting chemicals. The surroundings are everything else that can exchange energy with it, including the solvent, the container, and the air.
cards.note: In coffee-cup calorimetry the water is part of the surroundings, not the system.

cards.q: State the sign conventions for q and w for a thermodynamic system.
cards.a: q is positive when heat flows into the system (endothermic) and negative when heat flows out (exothermic). w is positive when work is done on the system, as in compression, and negative when the system expands and does work.

cards.q: State the first law of thermodynamics in equation form.
cards.a: ΔE = q + w: the change in internal energy equals heat added to the system plus work done on it. Because energy is conserved, q_system = -q_surroundings.

cards.q: State the expression for pressure-volume work and explain its sign.
cards.a: w = -PΔV at constant external pressure. When the system expands ΔV is positive, so w is negative, reflecting that the system does work on the surroundings.

cards.q: Explain in terms of bond energies why a reaction is exothermic.
cards.a: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy and forming bonds always releases it. If the bonds formed in the products release more energy than was needed to break the bonds in the reactants, the net energy change is negative.

cards.q: Explain why a beaker feels cold during an endothermic reaction in solution.
cards.a: The system absorbs energy from the solution and container, lowering their temperature. Heat then flows from your hand into the beaker, and the loss of energy from your skin is sensed as cold.

cards.q: Define heat and contrast it with temperature.
cards.a: Heat, q, is energy transferred because of a temperature difference and is measured in joules. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles and does not depend on how much sample is present.
cards.note: A large lukewarm tub of water contains far more thermal energy than a small very hot cup.

cards.q: Define specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity, and heat capacity.
cards.a: Specific heat capacity c is the energy to raise 1 gram by 1 K, in J/(g·K). Molar heat capacity uses 1 mole instead. Heat capacity C applies to an entire object and is in J/K.

cards.q: State the equation relating heat transferred to temperature change.
cards.a: q = mcΔT, where m is mass in grams, c is specific heat capacity in J/(g·K), and ΔT = T_final - T_initial. A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so either may be used for ΔT.
cards.note: A negative ΔT produces a negative q, correctly showing that the sample released energy.

cards.q: Determine the heat absorbed when 50.0 g of water is warmed from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C, given c = 4.18 J/(g·K).
Explain what a large specific heat capacity indicates about a substance.
cards.a: A large amount of energy is needed per gram to change its temperature, so it heats and cools slowly. Water's unusually high value of 4.18 J/(g·K) comes from its extensive hydrogen bonding.

cards.q: Predict which of two equal-mass samples absorbing equal heat undergoes the larger temperature change.
cards.a: The sample with the smaller specific heat capacity, because ΔT = q/(mc) is inversely proportional to c.

cards.q: Define calorimetry.
cards.a: The experimental measurement of heat flow, carried out by recording the temperature change of a known mass of surroundings whose specific heat capacity is known and applying q = mcΔT.

cards.q: Explain how a constant-pressure coffee-cup calorimeter measures the enthalpy change of a reaction.
cards.a: The reaction runs in solution open to the atmosphere, so heat flow at constant pressure equals ΔH. Measure the solution's temperature change, compute q_solution = mcΔT, and set q_rxn = -q_solution.
cards.hint: → what is measured, then two steps
cards.note: The mass used in q = mcΔT is the mass of the entire solution, not just the dissolved solute.

cards.q: Contrast a bomb calorimeter with a coffee-cup calorimeter.
cards.a: A bomb calorimeter is a sealed rigid vessel, so volume is constant, no PV work is done, and it measures ΔE rather than ΔH. Heat is found from q = C_cal ΔT using the calibrated heat capacity of the whole apparatus.

cards.q: State the relationship between the heat of the reaction and the heat gained by the solution.
cards.a: q_rxn = -q_solution. Energy released by the reaction is absorbed by the solution and vice versa, so the two are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
cards.note: Omitting this sign flip converts an exothermic result into an endothermic one and loses the point.

cards.q: State how to convert a measured q_rxn into a molar enthalpy of reaction.
cards.a: Divide q_rxn by the moles of the limiting reactant and convert to kilojoules: ΔH = q_rxn / n. Report the value as negative for an exothermic reaction, with units of kJ/mol.

cards.q: Decide the sign of q_rxn when the temperature of the calorimeter water rises.
cards.a: Negative. The water gained heat, so q_solution is positive, and q_rxn = -q_solution is negative; the reaction is exothermic.
cards.hint: → sign plus one step of reasoning

cards.q: Explain the simplifying assumptions made about the solution in coffee-cup calorimetry.
cards.a: The solution is assumed to have the density of pure water (1.00 g/mL) and the specific heat capacity of pure water (4.18 J/(g·K)), and the calorimeter and surroundings are assumed to absorb negligible heat.

cards.q: Explain how heat lost to the calorimeter and air affects a measured exothermic ΔH.
cards.a: Less of the released energy reaches the water, so the measured ΔT is too small and the calculated magnitude of q is too small. The reported ΔH is therefore less negative than the true value.

cards.q: Explain why a heating curve has flat plateaus.
cards.a: During a phase change all added energy goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions, raising potential energy rather than average kinetic energy. Temperature therefore stays constant until the phase change is complete.

cards.q: Define enthalpy of fusion and enthalpy of vaporization.
cards.a: ΔH_fus is the energy required to melt one mole of a solid at its melting point; ΔH_vap is the energy required to vaporize one mole of a liquid at its boiling point. Both are positive because both are endothermic.

cards.q: Explain why ΔH_vap is much larger than ΔH_fus for the same substance.
cards.a: Melting only loosens the particles enough to let them slide past one another, while vaporizing must separate them completely and overcome essentially all remaining intermolecular attraction.
cards.note: This is why the boiling plateau on a heating curve is far longer than the melting plateau.

cards.q: State the equation for the heat involved in a phase change.
cards.a: q = nΔH for the phase change, using moles and the molar enthalpy. There is no ΔT term because temperature is constant during a phase change, so q = mcΔT does not apply.
cards.note: Applying q = mcΔT across a plateau is a common error; ΔT there is zero.

cards.q: Contrast a cooling curve with a heating curve.
cards.a: The cooling curve is the mirror image: temperature falls through the single-phase regions and holds constant while freezing and condensing. Every q is negative because energy is released, and ΔH_freezing = -ΔH_fus.

cards.q: State how to find the total energy needed to convert ice below 0 °C into steam above 100 °C.
cards.a: Add the segments in order: mcΔT for the ice, nΔH_fus, mcΔT for the liquid water, nΔH_vap, then mcΔT for the steam. Each segment uses its own specific heat, and the two phase-change terms have no ΔT.

cards.q: Define enthalpy and enthalpy of reaction.
cards.a: Enthalpy H is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. ΔH_rxn is the heat absorbed or released when the reaction occurs as written at constant pressure, so ΔH = q at constant pressure.

cards.q: Explain how ΔH changes when a reaction is reversed or when its coefficients are multiplied.
cards.a: Reversing the reaction reverses the sign of ΔH. Multiplying every coefficient by a factor multiplies ΔH by that same factor, because ΔH is extensive and refers to the equation exactly as written.
cards.note: ΔH is per mole of reaction as written, so doubling the balanced equation doubles ΔH.

cards.q: Explain what the unit kilojoules per mole of reaction means for an enthalpy value.
cards.a: It is the energy change for one complete turn of the balanced equation as written, not per mole of any single substance. Changing the coefficients changes how much material one mole of reaction represents.

cards.q: Define a state function and name thermodynamic examples.
cards.a: A property whose value depends only on the current state of the system and not on the path taken to reach it. Enthalpy, internal energy, entropy, and free energy are state functions; heat and work are not.

cards.q: State the standard conditions implied by the degree symbol in ΔH°.
cards.a: Gases at 1 bar (about 1 atm), solutions at 1 M, each element in its most stable form, with data usually tabulated at 298 K.

cards.q: State how to calculate the enthalpy of a reaction from bond enthalpies.
cards.a: ΔH = Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds broken in the reactants) - Σ(bond enthalpies of bonds formed in the products), because breaking bonds is endothermic and forming bonds is exothermic.
cards.note: Reversing this to formed minus broken is the single most common bond-enthalpy error and flips the sign.

cards.q: Explain why a bond-enthalpy calculation gives only an approximate ΔH.
cards.a: Tabulated bond enthalpies are averages taken across many different molecules, and the method assumes every species is a gas. Intermolecular forces and any phase changes are ignored.

cards.q: Using bond enthalpies H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 243, H-Cl = 432 kJ/mol, determine ΔH for H2 + Cl2 → 2 HCl.
cards.a: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2(432) = 864 kJ. ΔH = 679 - 864 = -185 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

cards.q: Predict the sign of ΔH when the bonds formed in the products are stronger than the bonds broken in the reactants.
cards.a: Negative, meaning exothermic, because forming the stronger new bonds releases more energy than was required to break the weaker old ones.

cards.q: Explain why combustion reactions are strongly exothermic in terms of bonds.
cards.a: The C=O bonds in CO2 and the O-H bonds in H2O are very strong, releasing more energy on formation than is needed to break the weaker C-H, C-C, and O=O bonds in the fuel and oxygen.

cards.q: State Hess's law and justify it.
cards.a: The enthalpy change of an overall reaction equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of any set of steps that add up to that reaction. This works because enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH is independent of the path.

cards.q: State the rules for manipulating equations when applying Hess's law.
cards.a: Reversing an equation reverses the sign of its ΔH; multiplying an equation by a factor multiplies its ΔH by the same factor. Add the adjusted equations so unwanted species cancel, then add the adjusted ΔH values.
cards.note: Species cancel only if they match in phase; H2O(l) does not cancel H2O(g).

cards.q: Define the standard enthalpy of formation.
cards.a: ΔH°f is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions. Its units are kJ/mol.
cards.hint: → one sentence built around one mole

cards.q: State the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state.
cards.a: Zero. Examples with ΔH°f = 0 include O2(g), N2(g), Cl2(g), Br2(l), Hg(l), C(graphite), and Na(s).
cards.note: Only the most stable form qualifies, so O3(g), C(diamond), and Br2(g) do not have ΔH°f = 0.

cards.q: State the equation for the standard enthalpy of reaction from enthalpies of formation.
cards.a: ΔH°rxn = ΣnΔH°f(products) - ΣnΔH°f(reactants), where each n is the coefficient of that species in the balanced equation.
cards.note: Each ΔH°f must be multiplied by its coefficient; omitting n is a frequent AP arithmetic error.

cards.q: Using ΔH°f values of -74.8 (CH4), -393.5 (CO2), and -285.8 kJ/mol (H2O liquid), determine ΔH° for CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l).
cards.note: O2(g) contributes zero because it is an element in its standard state.

cards.q: Identify the standard states of bromine, mercury, carbon, and oxygen.
cards.a: Br2(l), Hg(l), C(graphite, solid), and O2(g). These are the most stable forms at about 1 bar and 298 K.

cards.q: Identify the features of a reaction energy diagram for an exothermic reaction.
cards.a: The reactants begin at a higher energy than the products; the curve climbs by Ea to the transition state and then falls to a product level below the starting level. ΔH is the negative drop from reactants to products.
